title: Al-Kahf: The Cave
intro: 18 days through Surah Al-Kahf, the Cave, and its four stories.

posts.display: Praise be to Allah Who hath revealed the Scripture unto His slave, and hath not placed therein any crookedness.
posts.display_original: ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَنزَلَ عَلَىٰ عَبْدِهِ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَلَمْ يَجْعَل لَّهُۥ عِوَجَا
posts.caption: Al-Kahf, "The Cave", is the eighteenth surah: Meccan, with 110 verses. Many Muslims read it every Friday, a practice based on hadith that promise light to those who do. It opens with praise, as only four other surahs do, and is built around four stories: the sleepers of the cave, the two gardens, Musa (Moses) and al-Khidr, and Dhul-Qarnayn.

The surah sets its theme early: the beauty of the earth is a test of who does best. Many modern teachers read the four stories as four trials: of faith in the cave, wealth in the gardens, knowledge with the Prophet Musa (Moses) and al-Khidr, and power with Dhul-Qarnayn. "Ornament" renders zinah, adornment.

The People of the Cave, ashab al-kahf, were young believers who fled a people that worshipped idols and took refuge in a cave. Their prayer for mercy from Allah's own presence and for right guidance is often recited as a du'a. A similar story is told in Christian tradition as the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus.

The sleepers are fityah, young men, and Allah says He increased them in guidance; commentators cite this to show that faith can grow. Allah lets them sleep in the cave for many years while their dog lies stretched at the entrance. Their exact number, the surah says, is best known to Allah.

According to the early biographer Ibn Ishaq, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was asked about the youths of the cave, a great traveller and the spirit, and promised an answer the next day without adding "if Allah wills". Revelation then paused for days. These verses are why Muslims say In sha Allah about plans for the future.

The second story is a parable of two men. One is given two rich vineyards ringed with date palms, with fields of crops between them. He grows proud of his wealth and imagines it will never end. "Coin for them a similitude" means "set out a parable for them".

posts.display: If only, when thou enteredst thy garden, thou hadst said: That which Allah willeth (will come to pass)! There is no strength save in Allah!
posts.display_original: وَلَوْلَآ إِذْ دَخَلْتَ جَنَّتَكَ قُلْتَ مَا شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِٱللَّهِ
posts.caption: His humbler friend tells the proud owner what he ought to have said on entering his garden: Ma sha Allah, "what Allah wills", and La quwwata illa billah, "there is no strength except in Allah". Many Muslims say Ma sha Allah when admiring something, a habit rooted partly in this verse. Soon after, the garden is ruined.

After the gardens, the surah draws the lesson. Wealth and children adorn worldly life, but "the good deeds which endure" (al-baqiyat as-salihat) are better. Some early commentators identified these lasting deeds with phrases of remembrance like SubhanAllah and Alhamdulillah; others with every good act.

The third story. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet Musa (Moses) learned of a servant of Allah who knew what he did not, and was told to seek him at the meeting of two seas (Pickthall's "two rivers"). He sets out with a young companion, named in hadith as Yusha' (Joshua).

At the meeting of the two seas, the Prophet Musa (Moses) finds a servant of Allah who was taught knowledge directly from Him. The Quran does not name him; hadith call him al-Khidr, "the green one". One of the greatest prophets now asks, with real humility, to become his student.

Al-Khidr warns the Prophet Musa (Moses) that he will not have the patience for what is to come, since he cannot know its hidden purpose. "Bear with" renders tasbir, from sabr, patience. Musa promises to be patient, and al-Khidr sets one condition: ask about nothing until he explains it himself.

Al-Khidr does three baffling things on their journey, including damaging a boat and rebuilding a wall for a town that refused them food. The Prophet Musa (Moses) protests each time, and they part. Then come the explanations, beginning with the boat: a flaw saved its poor owners from a king who was seizing ships by force.

The fourth story, of Dhul-Qarnayn, "the one with two horns", a righteous ruler whom Allah made strong on the earth. "A road" renders sabab, a means: he is given the means to reach what he seeks, and travels to the far west and east. Some linked him to Alexander the Great, others to the Persian king Cyrus; the Quran itself does not say.

Between two mountains, a people ask Dhul-Qarnayn for protection from Gog and Magog (Ya'juj and Ma'juj) and offer him payment. He declines the money, saying what Allah has given him is better, and asks only for their labour. Together they build a barrier of iron and molten copper.

With the barrier built, Dhul-Qarnayn takes no credit for himself: it is a mercy from his Lord. He adds that it will not stand forever; when Allah's promise comes, it will be levelled. In this story, power is held as a trust and used to protect others.

Near its end the surah turns to the Day of Judgment. These verses describe a striking kind of loss: people whose effort in this life went astray while they believed they were doing good. The verse that follows makes clear it means those who rejected their Lord's signs and the meeting with Him.

A famous image of the endlessness of Allah's words: if the sea were ink, it would run dry before they were exhausted, even with another sea added. A similar picture appears in Surah Luqman (31:27), where every tree on earth becomes a pen.

The last verse of Al-Kahf. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told to say he is a human being like everyone else, set apart only by revelation, whose heart is the oneness of Allah. The surah closes with a simple path: good deeds and worship of Allah alone. Thank you for reading Al-Kahf here.
